chapters.title: 35 South America: Farming, Mining and the Environment

passages.p1: South America has a strong agricultural industry. Many farmers still use old methods to grow potatoes and corn. But from the late 20th century, agricultural corporations used advanced technology to grow cash crops such as coffee, soybeans, bananas, and sugarcane.
passages.p2: Agricultural corporations received a lot of money from the government and from countries such as the United States and Japan. Coffee, soybeans, meat, sugar, and bioethanol are important exports. South American countries have a lot of minerals such as oil, copper, iron ore, bauxite, and rare metals.
passages.p3: The governments of South America worked hard to mine minerals, and their economies grew by exporting them. Japan imports a lot of iron ore and copper from South America. Mining and industry grew together, and now Brazil makes cars and airplanes.
passages.p4: Agriculture and industry are growing very quickly in South America, but many people are worried about environmental problems such as forest areas decreasing. After 1970, corporations cut down large areas of tropical rainforest in the Amazon Basin.
passages.p5: Corporations built roads, livestock farms, soybean fields, and sugarcane fields. Traditional farmers cut down trees for slash-and-burn agriculture, but they protected the forests. Corporations cut down many more trees than traditional farmers and destroyed the forests.
passages.p6: Farming and mining grew together in the Amazon Basin. There are many problems because of big farms and mining. Growing the same crops on the same land makes the soil poor. Crops don’t grow well, and agriculture is hard to continue.
passages.p7: Tropical rainforests have many kinds of plants and animals, but many of them are disappearing. Once they are gone, they will never return. Too much mining also destroys the environment. When the minerals are gone, the mining industry will also disappear.
